title: Multi-Container Apps with Compose
summary: Orchestrating a handful of related containers on one host, and recognizing exactly when you've outgrown it.

slides.markdown:
Most real apps aren't one container — they're a web server, an API, a database, and a cache, all needing to talk to each other. **Compose** describes that whole group in one YAML file and brings it up or down as a single unit with one command.

It's the right tool for local dev and small single-host deployments — and the wrong tool the moment you need multi-host resilience, which is where Kubernetes takes over.

slides.subTitle: One file, one multi-service app
slides.markdown:
Without Compose, running a multi-container app means remembering (or scripting) a long sequence of `docker run` commands with matching network and volume flags, in the right order, every time. Compose replaces that with one declarative YAML file — `docker compose up` reads it and creates every service, network, and volume it describes, wired together automatically.

It's the difference between a fragile shell script and a checked-in, reviewable definition of your whole local stack.

A compose file has three top-level building blocks:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: ./api
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: ["db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
volumes:
  db-data:
```

Each entry under `services` becomes one container; `volumes` declares named, persistent storage; and an implicit shared network is created automatically so services can reach each other by their service name (`api` can connect to `db:5432`).

slides.subTitle: Within a compose network
slides.markdown:
Compose automatically puts every service on the same default network and registers each service name in that network's DNS — so `api` can reach the database simply by connecting to hostname `db`, with no IP addresses hardcoded anywhere.

This is the same embedded-DNS mechanism a user-defined Docker bridge network provides; Compose just wires it up for you without any extra configuration.

slides.subTitle: Compose override files
slides.markdown:
Compose merges a base `docker-compose.yml` with an optional `docker-compose.override.yml` (loaded automatically) or an explicitly named file like `docker-compose.prod.yml`, letting you keep one shared base definition and layer environment-specific differences on top — mounting live source code locally, but not in a "prod-like" staging run.

This avoids duplicating the entire file per environment; only the actual differences need to be written down.

slides.subTitle: A web + API + DB stack
slides.markdown:
A typical three-service local stack:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: ./web
    ports: ["80:80"]
    depends_on: [api]
  api:
    build: ./api
    environment:
      - DB_HOST=db
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass
    volumes: ["db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
volumes:
  db-data:
```

One `docker compose up` brings up all three, wired together and ready, in the order their `depends_on` chain requires.

**Wrong belief:** "Compose works great for local dev, so we'll just run it on our production server too."

**Why it's wrong:** Compose has no concept of multiple hosts, no automatic failover if the one machine running it dies, no rolling updates, and no built-in self-healing. It's a single-host tool by design — production resilience needs something that reacts to a whole machine disappearing.

**Correct model:** Compose suits local dev and small, single-host, low-stakes deployments; multi-host resilience, rolling updates, or auto-healing need a real orchestrator.

slides.subTitle: The signals
slides.markdown:
Reach for Kubernetes when: you need to run across **more than one machine** for capacity or resilience, you need **zero-downtime rolling updates** instead of stop-then-start, you need **automatic recovery** when a container or whole node dies, or you're coordinating **many independently-deployed services** rather than one small fixed stack.

Until those needs show up concretely, Compose is simpler and genuinely the right tool — adopting Kubernetes before you need it just adds operational overhead for no benefit.
